title: p50-p99-storyboard-and-demo-notes
body:
Purpose: capture concise, demo-ready messages and scripts that show how Redwood converts latency SLOs into direct unit-economics wins. Focus on p50 and p99 storytelling (short tail + tail behavior), concrete demo scenarios, and a repeatable microbenchmark plan that sales/SEs can run in customer calls.

Audience: field SEs, product marketers, demo engineers, and sales reps who need fast, evidence-backed claims that we are “faster and cheaper” in ways customers care about.

High-level claim set (short):
- P50 latency drives developer-perceived speed; our p50 is X–Y% lower than typical managed endpoints for interactive assistants under realistic prompt mixes.
- P99 tail controls availability and perceived reliability during microbursts; our routing + KV cache + autoscaling keeps p99 under target without large reserved capacity.
- Unit cost per useful token falls when p50/p99-improvements reduce retry rates and when batching/caching are applied — present the counterfactual math to show net $/session savings.

Competitive frame: what to emphasize vs typical alternatives
- MajorCloud: strong raw throughput but requires high reserved capacity to hit p99; emphasize our smart routing + on-demand warm pools that reduce reserved spend for the same tail SLA.
- EdgeOps: good for small latency wins on short prompts; call out scale and consistency limitations with long-context workloads and retrieval-augmented flows.
- SelfHost: full control but large ops overhead and unpredictable kernel-level tuning; we sell the operational delta (SRE+runtime) as cost and time saved.

Key demo scenarios (scripts + expected observable metrics):
1) Live chat support microburst
   - Setup: 50 concurrent users ramping to 250 over 60s. Mixed prompt sizes (avg 120 tokens, 10% stream responses). Retrieval hits 30%.
   - What to show: p50 and p99 latency lines on a live graph, fallback events (if any), and per-route cost estimate.
   - Expected numbers (baseline vs Redwood example):
     * Baseline p50: 240ms -> Redwood p50: 120–150ms
     * Baseline p99: 3200ms -> Redwood p99: 600–900ms
     * Session-level cost delta: baseline $0.012/session -> Redwood $0.008/session (after batching & prefix cache)
   - Script highlights: start with a short prompt, then inject a surge of long-chained prompts. Point out how prefix cache eliminates repeated KV deserializations.

2) Batch embeddings job (throughput + cost)
   - Setup: 100k documents, 768-dim embeddings, target wall time < 2 hours for indexing.
   - What to show: tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and $/1000-embeddings comparison after autoscaling.
   - Expected numbers: throughput uplift 1.5–2x vs naive cloud endpoint due to continuous batching and efficient kernel path; net $/1000 embeddings 20–40% lower after queuing and dynamic pooling.

3) Retrieval-augmented agent (steady-state long context)
   - Setup: 8k context window with chunked retrieval; user-level avg response length 600 tokens.
   - What to show: end-to-end latency distribution, KV cache hit rate, and fallback to smaller quantized variant under pressure.
   - Expected numbers: p50 ~ 400–600ms; p99 ~ 1.2–1.8s with graceful fallback that keeps correctness within ±2% on evaluation seeds.

Microbenchmark methodology (repeatable):
- Workload definition: provide JSON workload files with prompt mixes (short/medium/long), streaming fraction, retrieval-hit fraction, and concurrency profile. Keep seeds for deterministic prompt generation.
- Hardware normalization: always report GPU type, batch size, and quantization profile. When comparing to public cloud numbers, show the raw GPU SKU and hourly price used in the comparator.
- Measurements to capture per run: p50, p90, p95, p99, tail events (retries/fallbacks), tokens/sec, token cost estimate, GPU utilization, and memory footprint.
- Run cadence: warm run (30s), steady run (5m), burst run (60s ramp). Repeat 3x and show median.

Proof-plan (what field teams can deliver quickly):
- On-call demo harness: a prebuilt Jupyter notebook + Prometheus dashboard that spins up a controlled load against customer-owned workload (or sample dataset). Script includes commands to toggle caching and routing policies.
- Quick-win artifact: a one-slide “how we saved $Xk/year” estimator that maps reduction in p99/failed-retry rate to saved developer cycles and infra spend.
- SE checklist for calls: bring the workbook, verify customer's baseline GPU SKU, run the 5-minute microbenchmark live, and commit to a follow-up report within 48 hours.

Customer-facing claim language (short, legal-light):
- "Our inference runtime reduces median response time by half on typical interactive workloads, while tail response time during bursts is kept to under 1s for most enterprise-grade prompts. This translates to lower per-session compute spend and fewer retries for users."
- Caveat line: "Results depend on workload shape, prompt lengths, and retrieval rates; we provide a tailored microbenchmark to validate impact on your workload."

Appendix: quick math example (per-session impact)
- Assumptions: avg session = 8 prompts, avg prompt -> 200 tokens generated, baseline retry rate during bursts = 5% (retries add 100% extra tokens on retry), Redwood retry rate = 1%.
- Baseline tokens/session = 8 * 200 * 1.05 = 1680 tokens. Redwood tokens/session = 8 * 200 * 1.01 = 1616 tokens.
- If price = $0.00006/token, baseline cost = $0.1008/session, Redwood = $0.09696/session. Saving = $0.00384/session (~3.8%). Multiply by 1M sessions/year => ~$3.8k/year. Add impact of lower reserved capacity for tail -> additional savings (example dependent).

Open items and experiments to run (owner tags):
- Measure real customer microburst patterns (Aisha) -> JIRA-GTM-987.
- Automate demo harness to flip caching on/off within live environment (Ben).
- Build one-pager that maps p50/p99 to developer productivity signals (Maya).

Notes to SEs (practical tips):
- Always collect the GPU SKU and a short sample trace from the customer before a deep-dive.
- When possible, run our warm run on the customer workload to show KV/prefix caching benefit; many customers misattribute wins solely to model size.
- Use the math appendix live: small percent improvements compound across millions of sessions.

End.
